top_choice_rationale: P002 (Autor, Hanson, Katz) recognises one empirical programme on how technology and trade shift labour demand and how adjustment is persistent and concentrated in particular places. Katz anchors the long-run wage-structure benchmark, Autor the task and trade-shock evidence, and Hanson the regional-adjustment evidence. The core work is mature (about three decades for the skill-premium and task work, over a decade for the trade-shock work), and it has been replicated and contested in the open. The citation should rest on the empirical findings, not the whole task framework (Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane) and not a final verdict on China-shock magnitudes. Costs I accept: Dorn is excluded by the three-name cap, shift-share identification and persistence are still debated, and the work could be read as two strands joined by Autor. P001 (Helpman, Melitz) is a close second. It has a cleaner originating model and long confirmation, but it leaves out Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, and its welfare magnitudes depend on Pareto and CES assumptions. I rank it above no award because it is a mature and defensible achievement. I rank P000 last because both proposals meet the bar. I treat round-1 and round-2 support counts as information about which arguments were examined, not as evidence of merit.
recusal_note: None apparent from profile. No co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz, Dorn, Helpman or Melitz is documented. My field, empirical labour economics, is close to P002, which I treat as a reason for caution about over-weighting familiarity and not as evidence of merit. As chair I gave the 2021 presentation speech, and my 2013 class-size paper is cited in that scientific background. That is a connection to a neighbouring prize, not to any credited name. Conflicts are disclosed, not adjudicated.
